lead: Mobile security is the set of threats and the controls that answer them, grouped by where the attacker sits: in your app's code and data, on the network between phone and server, or in the handset itself. Every app you build carries a wallet's worth of risk, because it holds user data, talks to a server and sits in a pocket. The controls are unglamorous — least privilege, encrypted storage, TLS, a screen lock, a remote wipe — and together they decide how much a lost phone or a curious user actually costs.
prereq: You need the file and preference storage of Chapter 4.2 and the wireless risks of Unit 1, Wireless LANs.

blocks.text: Group mobile threats by where the attacker stands. The app layer is your code and the data it stores. The network layer is traffic between the phone and your server. The device layer is the physical handset and the person holding it.

items: App layer: a repackaged APK carrying malware, a permission the feature never uses, a secret printed to the log, a private file written to shared storage, data leaking through an implicit intent.
Network layer: plain HTTP, a fake free Wi-Fi hotspot that copies traffic (an evil twin, see Unit 1, Wireless LANs), a TLS setting that trusts every certificate.
Device layer: a lost phone with no screen lock, a shoulder surfer reading a notification, an automatic backup that copies private files to a laptop.

blocks.text: A useful habit is the attacker's view: what does the attacker gain, and what does it cost them? A stolen unlocked phone costs nothing to read. The same phone behind a 6-digit PIN with remote wipe costs time, and the data may be erased before it is read.

OWASP publishes a Mobile Top 10, a list of common mobile weakness categories. Treat it as a review checklist. The entries change between editions, so read the current list rather than memorising an old one.

sections.h3: Least privilege and the app sandbox

blocks.text: Android gives each installed app its own Linux user id. Its internal files are readable only by that user id. This is the app sandbox. It stops one app reading another's files, and it is the reason internal storage is the default home for private data.

The sandbox says nothing about what the app itself may do. That is the permission system. Each dangerous capability — camera, contacts, location, microphone — is a permission declared in the manifest. From Android 6.0 (API 23) the dangerous ones are granted at runtime, one prompt at a time.

items: Before using the feature, check the current grant with ContextCompat.checkSelfPermission.
If it is not granted, call requestPermissions, showing a one-line reason first.
Handle onRequestPermissionsResult: on grant, do the work; on refusal, hide or disable the feature.
Re-check at every use. The user can revoke the permission from Settings at any time.

blocks.text: Least privilege means asking only for what the feature needs. An app that picks one photo can use the system photo picker and request no storage permission at all. Fewer permissions means less damage if the app is later compromised, and fewer users abandoning the install.

sections.h3: Data at rest and data in transit

blocks.text: Data at rest means stored bytes: files, SQLite rows, SharedPreferences. Internal storage is private but not encrypted by your app. Sensitive values — access tokens, card references, health notes — should be encrypted before they are written.

The Android Keystore holds keys, not data. You generate a key inside it, and the key material never leaves the keystore; you receive a Cipher object that uses it. On many devices the key sits in dedicated hardware, so an image of the flash memory cannot be decrypted on another machine.
Bad places for a secret: hardcoded in the source, printed with Log.d, or written to world-readable external storage. An APK can be unzipped and its strings read.
Data in transit means bytes on the wire. Use HTTPS, which is HTTP inside TLS. TLS gives encryption, integrity, and a check that the server certificate chains to a trusted authority.

Two common mistakes. A custom TrustManager that accepts all certificates turns TLS into decoration. And HTTPS says nothing about stored data: both the server and the phone hold plaintext at the ends of the connection.

Certificate pinning fixes the acceptable certificate or public key inside the app. It defeats an attacker holding a rogue authority certificate, at the cost of a forced app update whenever you rotate the key.
The device layer holds the cheapest controls. A screen lock — PIN, pattern, password or fingerprint — turns a stolen phone from an open book into a locked box.

blocks.where: N is the number of possible numeric PINs and d is the number of digits; each digit is 0-9.

blocks.text: Length beats cleverness. A 4-digit PIN has 10⁴ = 10,000 combinations; a 6-digit PIN has 10⁶ = 1,000,000, a hundred times more. A lockout delay after a few wrong tries matters more than either.

Remote wipe lets the owner erase the handset over the network, through Find My Device or an enterprise MDM (mobile device management) server. It works only while the phone is online; a thief who stays on airplane mode keeps the data.

Other device-level controls: auto-lock after about 30 s, hide notification content on the lock screen, exclude sensitive files from auto backup using android:allowBackup and backup rules, and set android:usesCleartextTraffic="false" so a bug cannot silently fall back to HTTP.

figure.caption: The same app is attacked at three places. Notice that the two shaded leaves are the controls most often skipped in student projects: certificate checking and remote wipe.

spec.aria: The tree groups mobile security into app, network and device layers, with controls such as permissions, encrypted storage, TLS, screen lock and remote wipe.

examples.question: A wallet app uses a 4-digit PIN. How many PINs are possible? At 10 guesses per second with no lockout, how long does trying all of them take? If the app locks for 30 s after every 5 wrong guesses, what is the approximate total time to try all 10,000 PINs?
steps: Each digit runs 0-9, four places, so the number of PINs is N = 10⁴ = 10,000.
No lockout: 10,000 guesses ÷ 10 guesses per second = 1,000 s.
With lockout: 10,000 ÷ 5 = 2,000 groups of five wrong guesses.
Lock time = 2,000 × 30 s = 60,000 s. The 30 s wait is not guessing time, so guessing time stays 1,000 s.
examples.answer: 10,000 PINs; 1,000 s (16 min 40 s) with no lockout; about 61,000 s ≈ 16.94 h with the 30 s lockout.
examples.check:
pins = 10**4
rate = 10
t_plain = pins / rate
groups = pins / 5
lock = groups * 30
t_total = t_plain + lock
print(pins)
print(t_plain)
print(lock)
print(t_total)
print(round(t_total / 3600, 2))

traps: HTTPS protects data on the wire only. Local files and SharedPreferences on the phone still need encryption or a keystore key.
A permission written in the manifest is not a permission granted. Runtime grants can be revoked, so check before every use.
The app sandbox protects one app's files from other apps on a healthy device; it does not protect against a rooted phone or a backup that copies the files out.
Full-device encryption protects data when the phone is off or locked, not while it is unlocked with the app running.
Pinning and 'trust all certificates' look like TLS settings but do opposite jobs; the examiner often asks which one is the vulnerability.

quiz.q: State the three layers of the mobile threat model and give one control for each.
quiz.a: App layer (permissions, sandbox, encrypted storage); network layer (TLS, certificate pinning); device layer (screen lock, remote wipe, auto-lock).

quiz.q: Why does the app sandbox stop App A from reading App B's private files on a normal phone, and why can it fail on a rooted phone?
quiz.a: Each app runs under its own Linux user id, and the file permissions on internal storage allow only that user id. Root gives a process the highest privilege, so file permissions no longer bind it, and any file can be read.

quiz.q: A 6-digit PIN, 10 guesses per second, lockout of 30 s after every 5 wrong guesses. Find the total time to try all PINs, in hours.
An app declares READ_CONTACTS and INTERNET but only needs to open the phone's e-mail app to send a feedback message. What is wrong and what should change?
quiz.a: It asks for contacts it never reads, breaking least privilege and scaring users at install. Sending mail needs no contacts permission and can be done with an implicit intent to an e-mail app, as in Chapter 5.1. Drop READ_CONTACTS; keep INTERNET only if the app itself uses the network.

quiz.q: Distinguish data at rest from data in transit, with one control for each.
quiz.a: At rest is stored bytes (files, SQLite, preferences); control: encryption with a Keystore-held key. In transit is bytes on the network; control: HTTPS with TLS and certificate checking.

quiz.q: A user loses a phone that is switched off and not connected. Which control fails and which still helps?
quiz.a: Remote wipe fails because the phone never receives the command. The screen lock and device encryption still help: without the PIN the flash contents stay encrypted.

quiz.q: Give one benefit and one cost of certificate pinning in a production app.
quiz.a: Benefit: an attacker with a rogue certificate authority cannot impersonate the server. Cost: when the server key rotates, every installed app version with the old pin fails until it is updated, so you need a backup pin and a release plan.

quiz.q: What does least privilege mean for an Android app?
quiz.a: The app requests only the permissions its current features actually use, and no more.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real review checklists now come from OWASP MASVS, which splits controls into storage, crypto, auth, network, platform interaction and code quality, and pairs each with a test. Hardware-backed key attestation lets a server verify that a signing key really lives in a phone's secure element, which is how banking apps detect cloned devices. Play Integrity and its iOS equivalent report whether a device is rooted or an app is repackaged. Passkeys replace the PIN with a key pair unlocked by the phone's biometric. Search next for 'OWASP MASVS', 'Android Keystore attestation' and 'certificate pinning rotation'.
